title: Unit 5f - Inheritance/Polymorphism Details
summary: Title slide introducing the Inheritance and Polymorphism Details unit for CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 5f - Inheritance/Polymorphism Details. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. This unit covers advanced topics in inheritance and polymorphism including access specifiers, vtables, design patterns, and practical design examples.
notes_text: This unit builds on Units 5d (Inheritance) and 5e (Polymorphism) to cover the remaining details and best practices for using these OOP mechanisms effectively.

title: Public, Private, Protected - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the three access specifiers and their interaction with inheritance.
main_text: Public, Private, Protected. This section covers how the three C++ access specifiers interact with inheritance to control member visibility across class hierarchies.
notes_text: Understanding the interplay between access specifiers (public, private, protected) and inheritance type (public, private, protected) is essential for designing proper class hierarchies.

title: Protected Members
summary: Introduces the protected access specifier, which allows derived class access but blocks third-party access, unlike private.
main_text: Private members of a base class cannot be accessed directly by a derived class member function. Code for print_grade_report() would not compile since 'name_' is private to class Person. Base class can declare variables with protected storage class which means: Private to any object or code not inheriting from the base (i.e. private to any 3rd party). Public to any derived (child) class, which can access directly. Example: If Person has private name_ and id_, Student's print_grade_report() cannot use name_ directly. But if Person changes those to protected, then Student can access name_ directly in its methods.
notes_text: Protected is the middle ground between public and private. It maintains encapsulation from external code while giving derived classes direct access to base members. This avoids the overhead of going through getters/setters within the class hierarchy, though some argue it breaks encapsulation too much.

title: Public, Protected, and Private Access
summary: Summarizes how derived classes see base members: public/protected are accessible, private is not, regardless of inheritance type.
main_text: Derived class sees base class members using the base class' specification. If Base class said it was public or protected, the derived class can access it directly. If Base class said it was private, the derived class cannot access it directly. Three cases illustrated: (1) Private Base Members: Neither derived class nor 3rd party can access, regardless of how the class was inherited. (2) Public Base Members: Both derived class and 3rd party can access, regardless of inheritance type. (3) Protected Base Members: Derived class CAN access (checkmark), but 3rd party CANNOT access (X mark), regardless of inheritance type.
notes_text: This is the foundational rule: the base class' own declaration of a member as public, protected, or private determines what the derived class itself can see. The inheritance type (public/protected/private) only affects how EXTERNAL code sees the inherited members, not the derived class itself.

images.description: Three-column diagram showing access rules for private, public, and protected base members. Each column shows a Base Class box connected to a Derived Class box and a 3rd party box. X marks and checkmarks indicate access permissions.

title: Public/Private/Protected Inheritance
summary: Explains how the inheritance type keyword controls how 3rd parties and grandchild classes see inherited public base members.
main_text: public/protected/private inheritance before the base class name indicates HOW the public base class members are viewed by clients (those outside) of the derived class. Inheriting publicly means: public and protected base class members STAY public and protected (respectively) in the child class. So, 3rd parties of the child class can see/use the publicly inherited members, and grandchildren classes can use the protected members. Inheriting protected-ly means: public and protected base class members are accessible to the child and grandchild classes, but no base class members are accessible to 3rd parties. Private inheritance means: public and protected base class members are accessible to the child class only. No base class members are accessible to grandchild classes or 3rd party clients. Example: Student : public Person allows s1.get_name() to work. Faculty : private Person causes f1.get_name() to fail.
notes_text: The inheritance type acts as a filter on inherited member visibility. Public inheritance preserves the base access levels. Protected inheritance downgrades public to protected. Private inheritance downgrades everything to private. Note that private members of the base are ALWAYS inaccessible to derived, regardless of inheritance type.

title: Inheritance Access Table
summary: Provides a decision table and guidelines for choosing public, private, or protected inheritance based on access needs.
main_text: Inherit publicly if you want 3rd party clients to call base class functions/methods that you inherited on your class. Derive as private if you want to use the base class functions/methods you inherited to implement your INTERNAL workings, but not allow 3rd party clients to call them. Derive as protected more rarely, for the same reasons as private inheritance, but also allow grandchild classes to use and call the base class methods you inherit. Access table: External client access to Base class members is always the more restrictive of either the base declaration or how the base is inherited. The table shows: Inherited as Public with Public base = Public, Protected base = Protected, Private base = Private. Inherited as Protected with Public base = Protected, Protected base = Protected, Private base = Private. Inherited as Private with Public base = Private, Protected base = Private, Private base = Private.
notes_text: The 'more restrictive' rule is the key principle. Take the more restrictive of the two access levels (base declaration and inheritance type) to determine the effective access level for external code. This table is essential for exams.

images.description: A 3x3 table showing inherited access levels. Rows are inheritance type (Public, Protected, Private). Columns are base member declaration (Public, Protected, Private). Cells show the resulting effective access level.

title: Public/Private/Protected Cases
summary: Worked example showing three child classes inheriting from a Base with public, protected, and private functions under different inheritance types.
main_text: Base Class has public void f1(), protected void f2(), and private void f3(). ChildA : public Base - child can call f1() (checkmark), f2() (checkmark), f3() (X). Grandchild GCA : public ChildA - g1() can call f1() (checkmark), f2() (checkmark), f3() (X). 3rd party main() can call a.f1() (checkmark), a.f2() (X), a.f3() (X). ChildB : protected Base - child can call f1() (checkmark), f2() (checkmark), f3() (X). Grandchild GCB - can call f1() (checkmark), f2() (checkmark), f3() (X). 3rd party: ALL X (f1, f2, f3 all inaccessible). ChildC : private Base - child can call f1() (checkmark), f2() (checkmark), f3() (X). Grandchild GCC - ALL X. 3rd party: ALL X. How a grandchild class or 3rd party sees what is inherited is the MORE RESTRICTIVE of how the base class declared it or how the derived class inherited.
notes_text: This comprehensive example shows every combination. The key patterns: (1) private base members are always inaccessible to derived, (2) the child itself always sees public and protected base members, (3) the inheritance type only affects grandchildren and 3rd parties, (4) private inheritance cuts off access at the grandchild level.

images.description: Three-column layout showing Base class at top with f1 (public), f2 (protected), f3 (private). Three child classes below (public, protected, private inheritance) each with grandchild and 3rd party access checks marked with checkmarks and X marks.

title: When to Inherit Privately
summary: Demonstrates when private inheritance is useful using a Queue inheriting from List, to hide List methods from users.
main_text: If public: Outside user can call the base List functions and break the Queue order. If private: hide the base class public function, so users can only call derived class interface. If protected: hide the base class public and protected functions except to derived and friend classes. For protected or private inheritance, the relationship is 'implemented-in-terms-of-a' or 'implemented-as'. Queue 'implemented in-terms-of' List. Example: class List has public insert(int loc, int val), size(), get(int loc), erase(int loc). class Queue : public List (or private List) wraps these: push_back(int val) calls insert(size(), val), front() calls get(0), pop_front() calls erase(0). Problem with public: q1.insert(0,9) is allowed, which can break queue ordering! Private inheritance prevents this.
notes_text: This is the classic motivation for private inheritance. A Queue is not a List (is-a doesn't hold), but it is implemented using a List. Public inheritance would expose List's arbitrary insert/erase methods, breaking the Queue's FIFO invariant. Private inheritance gives Queue internal access while hiding List's interface from users.

title: Polymorphism and Private Inheritance
summary: Warns that private/protected inheritance breaks type compatibility, preventing base pointers from referencing derived objects.
main_text: Warning: If private or protected inheritance is used, the derived class is no longer type-compatible with the base class. You can't have a base class pointer reference a derived object. Example: Person has virtual void print_info(). Student : public Person works fine. Faculty : private Person causes problems. In main(): Person *q; q = s (a Student pointer) works because Student publicly inherits Person. q = f (a Faculty pointer) won't work because Faculty privately inherits Person. Also, given class Queue : private LinkedList, you cannot do LinkedList *p = new Queue() - this is invalid. Summary: Generally, public inheritance is the most common and useful.
notes_text: This is a critical limitation of private/protected inheritance. Polymorphism REQUIRES public inheritance because the compiler needs to know that the derived type can safely be treated as the base type. Private inheritance intentionally hides this relationship, making polymorphic usage impossible.

title: Warning: Multiple Inheritance
summary: Warns against multiple inheritance in C++ due to the diamond problem, where ambiguous member access arises.
main_text: C++ allows multiple inheritance but it is NOT usually recommended. The diamond problem: Animal has int getWeight() and private int weight. Tiger : public Animal inherits weight. Lion : public Animal inherits weight. Liger : public Tiger, public Lion inherits from both. What happens for the following code? Liger x; int wt = x.getWeight(); The problem: Liger has TWO copies of Animal's weight member (one via Tiger, one via Lion). The call x.getWeight() is ambiguous because the compiler doesn't know which Animal's getWeight() to call. The class layout shows Class Liger containing both int Tiger::weight and int Lion::weight.
notes_text: The diamond problem is the classic argument against multiple inheritance. Most modern languages (Java, C#) avoid it entirely, offering interfaces instead. C++ provides virtual inheritance as a workaround, but it adds complexity. The general recommendation is to avoid multiple inheritance in C++.

images.description: Diamond inheritance diagram: Animal at top, Tiger and Lion inherit from Animal, Liger inherits from both Tiger and Lion. A class layout box shows Liger containing both Tiger::weight and Lion::weight, illustrating the duplication problem.

title: Summary: Inheritance, Composition, and Private Inheritance
summary: Summarizes when to use public inheritance (is-a), composition (has-a), and private/protected inheritance (implemented-in-terms-of).
main_text: Summary: Public Inheritance defines an 'is-a' relationship. Composition defines a 'has-a' relationship. Private/Protected Inheritance defines an 'implemented-as' or 'implemented-in-terms-of' relationship. Use public inheritance mainly when we want to add or specialize behavior and a true 'is-a' relationship holds for the relationship of base to derived. Use composition or private inheritance when reuse is the main desire. Example: Queue via Composition uses a private List mylist member with wrapper methods: push_back calls mylist.insert(size(), val), front() calls mylist.get(0), pop_front() calls mylist.pop(0), size() calls mylist.size().
notes_text: This summary slide provides the decision framework for choosing between the three approaches. The key insight: is-a => public inheritance (polymorphism possible). has-a => composition (most flexible). implemented-in-terms-of => private inheritance or composition (composition usually preferred).

title: Best Practices and Other Details - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing best practices, design principles, and implementation details for inheritance and polymorphism.
main_text: Best Practices and Other Details. This section covers OO design goals, SOLID principles, vtable mechanics, and practical design examples.
notes_text: This section transitions from syntax and mechanics to design philosophy and implementation details.

title: General OO Design Goal: Loose Coupling
summary: Reiterates that OO design seeks to reduce coupling by creating well-defined interfaces that allow swappable implementations.
main_text: Coupling refers to how much components depend on each other's implementation details (i.e. how much work it is to remove one component and drop in a new implementation of it). Low coupling (good) vs. Tight coupling (not so good): Replacing a new battery in your car (low coupling) vs. Replacing a new engine in your car (tight coupling). Adding a USB device to your laptop (low coupling) vs. Replacing the CPU in your laptop (tight coupling). OO Design seeks to reduce coupling as much as possible by creating well-defined interfaces to update (write) or access (read) the state of an object, and allowing alternate implementations that do NOT require interface changes.
notes_text: Loose coupling is the overarching design goal that motivates encapsulation, abstract interfaces, and polymorphism. When code depends only on interfaces rather than concrete implementations, individual components can be modified, replaced, or extended independently.

title: OO Design Principles (SOLID)
summary: Introduces the SOLID principles: Single-Responsibility and Open/Closed, as key guidelines for OO software design.
main_text: These are a few principles from what some developers refer to as the 5 SOLID principles. Single-Responsibility: A class (or even a function) should generally have only one responsibility (e.g. a product, a user, a quadrilateral, a linked list, etc.). Open/closed rule: A class should be open to extension but closed to modification. A class should be designed so that its behavior can be changed through inheritance/polymorphism, not modification. Feel free to search online for more readings. There's not one agreed upon set of principles and even how various principles are applied may be a subject of debate.
notes_text: SOLID stands for Single-responsibility, Open-closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, and Dependency inversion. Only S and O are covered here. The Open/Closed principle directly relates to inheritance: you extend behavior by creating new derived classes rather than modifying existing base classes.

title: Deeper Investigation - Resources
summary: Provides links and resources for further study on design patterns, the Open/Closed principle, and C++ inheritance FAQ.
main_text: Design patterns: Common OO structures and uses of inheritance/polymorphism. Resource: https://sourcemaking.com/design_patterns. Open/closed rule: Resource: http://butunclebob.com/ArticleS.UncleBob.PrinciplesOfOod. General guidelines and FAQ: https://isocpp.org/faq - Scroll to 'Classes and Inheritance' section.
notes_text: These resources provide depth beyond what the lecture covers. The isocpp.org FAQ is particularly valuable as the authoritative C++ reference for inheritance best practices.

title: VTables and VPtrs - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing how polymorphism works under the hood through vtables and vptrs.
main_text: VTables and VPtrs. How polymorphism works under the hood. This section explains the compiler-generated virtual function table (vtable) mechanism that enables dynamic dispatch at runtime.
notes_text: Understanding vtables is important for understanding the performance implications of virtual functions and why polymorphism requires pointers/references.

title: VTables
summary: Explains the vtable mechanism: compiler creates a function pointer table per class, and each object has a vptr pointing to its class vtable.
main_text: The compiler creates a table for each class with an entry for each virtual function (aka vtable). Each entry points to the appropriate function code to call. Each object has an extra data member (vptr) that points to the vtable for its class. Example with CollegeStudent (abstract), TrojanStudent, and CSTrojanStudent hierarchy. CollegeStudent vtable has take_test -> 0x0 (no implementation, pure virtual) and play_sports -> 0x0. TrojanStudent vtable has take_test -> 0x4001c0 (TrojanStudent's implementation) and play_sports -> 0x400284. CSTrojanStudent vtable has take_test -> 0x403e78 (CSTrojanStudent's override) and play_sports -> 0x400284 (same as TrojanStudent, inherited). Each object's vtable_ptr points to its class's specific vtable.
notes_text: The vtable is the implementation mechanism that makes dynamic binding possible. Key observations: (1) there is one vtable per class, not per object, (2) each object has a hidden vptr member that points to its class's vtable, (3) inherited virtual functions that are not overridden share the same function pointer as the parent, (4) pure virtual functions have 0x0 entries, preventing direct calls.

images.description: Three vtable diagrams showing CollegeStudent (0x0 entries for pure virtuals), TrojanStudent (concrete function addresses), and CSTrojanStudent (overridden take_test with different address, inherited play_sports with same address). Each class's object layout shows vtable_ptr, name, and class-specific members, with dashed arrows from vtable_ptr to the corresponding vtable.

title: Example of Calling Virtual Functions
summary: Traces virtual function calls through vtables showing how runtime dispatch follows the vptr to find the correct function.
main_text: Calling a non-virtual function always goes to the same code (known at compile time/statically). Calling a virtual function requires following the vtable ptr at runtime (dynamically) to find the correct function to call. Example: Three objects s (TrojanStudent at 0x5510), cs1 (CSTrojanStudent at 0x5530), cs2 (CSTrojanStudent at 0x5570). void f1(CollegeStudent* s) { cout << s->get_name(); s->take_test(); s->play_sports(); }. f1(&s) follows s's vtable_ptr to TrojanStudent vtable, calling TrojanStudent::take_test(). f1(&cs1) follows cs1's vtable_ptr to CSTrojanStudent vtable, calling CSTrojanStudent::take_test(). Both cs1 and cs2 share the same CSTrojanStudent vtable but are different objects at different addresses.
notes_text: This trace shows the runtime mechanism in action. get_name() is non-virtual so it always calls the same function. take_test() and play_sports() are virtual, so the runtime follows the vptr to the appropriate vtable. Note that cs1 and cs2 both point to the SAME vtable (one per class), but they are distinct objects with different data.

images.description: Three object memory layouts (s, cs1, cs2) each with vtable_ptr pointing to their respective class vtables. Pink dashed arrows trace the vtable lookup path for virtual function calls. Each vtable shows function addresses for take_test and play_sports.

title: An Inheritance and Polymorphism Design Example - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing a practical design example using inheritance and polymorphism in a game context.
main_text: An Inheritance and Polymorphism Design Example. This section walks through designing a monster game system, comparing approaches without and with polymorphism.
notes_text: This extended example demonstrates the design thinking process for choosing between data members, inheritance without polymorphism, and full polymorphism with virtual functions.

title: A Game of Monsters
summary: Introduces a game design problem with three monster types, each worth different points, asking how to organize the Monster classes.
main_text: Consider a video game with a heroine who has a score and fights 3 different types of monsters {A, B, C}. Upon slaying a monster you get a different point value: 10 pts for monster A, 20 pts for monster B, 30 pts for monster C. You can check if you've slayed a monster via an 'isDead()' call on a monster and then get the value to be added to the heroine's score via 'getScore()'. The game maintains objects for the heroine and the monsters. How would you organize your Monster class(es) and its data members?
notes_text: This slide poses the design challenge that will be explored over the next several slides. The key question is whether to use a type field, a value data member, or inheritance to differentiate monster types.

title: Using Type Data Member
summary: First approach: using a type integer to distinguish monsters, but this tightly couples the Monster class to specific types.
main_text: Can use a 'type' data member and code. Con: Adding new monster types requires modifying the Monster class code as does changing point totals. The Monster class has int _type (0=A, 1=B, 2=C) and getValue() uses if/else: if(_type == 0) return 10; else if(_type == 1) return 20; else return 30;. The Player class has addToScore(int val) { _score += val; }. The game loop iterates over monsters, checks isDead(), and adds the score: p.addToScore(monsters[i]->getValue()). The problem with this approach is that adding a new monster type D would require modifying getValue() with another if/else branch.
notes_text: This approach violates the Open/Closed Principle. Every time a new monster type is added, the existing Monster class must be modified. The if/else chain is a code smell that often indicates inheritance would be a better solution.

title: Using Score Data Member
summary: Second approach: storing the point value as a data member, decoupling the Monster class from specific type knowledge.
main_text: Can use a 'value' data member and code. Pro: Monster class is now decoupled from new types or changes to point values. The Monster class has int _value and constructor Monster(int val) : _value(val) { }. getValue() simply returns _value. In main(), monsters are created with their point values: monsters[0] = new Monster(10) for Type A, monsters[1] = new Monster(20) for Type B. The game loop remains the same: if(monsters[i]->isDead()) p.addToScore(monsters[i]->getValue()). This approach removes the if/else chain and makes Monster independent of specific types.
notes_text: This is a significant improvement over the type field approach. The Monster class no longer needs to know about specific monster types. New types can be added just by creating new Monster objects with different values. However, this only works when behavior differences can be captured as data.

title: Using Inheritance
summary: Notes that when the problem mentions different 'types', inheritance is likely a good solution, and prefers distinguishing types at creation time.
main_text: Go back to the requirements: 'Consider a video game with a heroine who has a score and fights 3 different types of monsters {A, B, C}'. Anytime you see 'types', 'kinds', etc., an inheritance hierarchy is probably a viable and good solution. Anytime you find yourself writing big if..elseif..else statements to determine the type of something, inheritance hierarchy is probably a good solution. Usually prefer to distinguish types at creation and not with if..else statements in the class. The Monster class still has getValue() returning _value, but the monster types are distinguished at creation: monsters[0] = new Monster(10) for Type A, monsters[1] = new Monster(20) for Type B.
notes_text: This slide provides two important design heuristics: (1) when the problem domain uses words like 'types' or 'kinds', think inheritance, (2) when you find yourself writing type-checking if/else chains, refactor to use polymorphism. The distinction should happen at object creation time, not in runtime type checks.

title: Is Polymorphism Needed?
summary: Shows that sometimes data members suffice, but when scoring depends on type-specific behavior (not just data), polymorphism is needed.
main_text: Sometimes a data member solves the issue! Other times, data is not enough and code is needed. Consider if the score of a monster is not just hard coded based on type but type and other data attributes. If Monster type A is slain with a single shot, your points are multiplied by the base score and their amount of time they are running around on the screen. However, Monster type B alternates between berserk mode and normal mode and you get different points based on what mode they are in when you slay them. These are fundamentally different scoring algorithms that cannot be captured by a simple data member.
notes_text: This is the pivot point in the design example. When behavior differs across types (not just data), a data member approach breaks down and polymorphism becomes necessary. MonsterA needs a time-based multiplier calculation while MonsterB needs a mode-based calculation. These are different algorithms that belong in different classes.

title: Using Polymorphism - Separate Classes Problem
summary: Shows that creating unrelated MonsterA and MonsterB classes fails because they can't be stored in a single container.
main_text: Can you just create different classes? Not really, can't store them around in a single container/array. class MonsterA has isDead() and int getValue() with code for multipliers and head shots. class MonsterB has isDead() and int getValue() with code for berserker mode. In main(): You can't have a single array of 'Monsters'. Need separate arrays: MonsterA* monsterAs = new MonsterA*[numMonsters]; MonsterB* monsterBs = new MonsterB*[numMonsters];. This defeats the purpose since you need separate loops and separate handling code for each type.
notes_text: Without inheritance, each monster type is an independent class with no shared base. This means no heterogeneous collection, no shared interface, and duplicated game loop logic. This motivates the inheritance solution.

title: Using Polymorphism - Static Binding Problem
summary: Shows that inheritance without virtual functions fails due to static binding: Monster::getValue() is always called instead of derived versions.
main_text: Will this work? No, static binding! Will only call Monster::getValue() and never MonsterA::getValue() or MonsterB::getValue(). class Monster has a non-virtual int getValue() with generic code. MonsterA : public Monster overrides getValue() with multiplier code. MonsterB : public Monster overrides getValue() with berserker mode code. Monster** monsters = new Monster*[numMonsters]; can store MonsterA and MonsterB objects. But when iterating and calling monsters[i]->getValue(), static binding means Monster::getValue() is called every time because the pointer type is Monster*.
notes_text: This is the step before the final solution. Inheritance alone is not enough; without the virtual keyword, the compiler uses static binding based on the pointer type (Monster*), not the actual object type. The fix is simple: add 'virtual' to Monster::getValue().

title: Using Polymorphism - Dynamic Binding Solution
summary: Shows the correct solution: making getValue() a pure virtual function enables dynamic binding and easy extensibility.
main_text: Will this work? Yes, Dynamic binding! Now I can add new Monster types without changing any Monster classes. Only the creation code needs to change. class Monster has virtual int getValue() = 0 (pure virtual). MonsterA : public Monster implements int getValue() with code for multipliers and head shots. MonsterB : public Monster implements int getValue() with code for berserker mode. Monster** monsters = new Monster*[numMonsters]; monsters[0] = new MonsterA (Type A Monster); monsters[1] = new MonsterB (Type B Monster). The game loop: while(1) { for(int i=0; i < numMonsters; i++) { if(monsters[i]->isDead()) p.addToScore(monsters[i]->getValue()); } }. Each call to getValue() dynamically dispatches to the correct derived implementation.
notes_text: This is the complete solution. Making getValue() pure virtual (= 0) makes Monster abstract (can't create Monster objects directly) and forces each derived class to provide its own implementation. Dynamic binding ensures the correct getValue() is called based on the actual object type. Adding a MonsterC type requires only creating a new class and updating the creation code.

title: Specific Design Patterns - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing specific design patterns that use class hierarchies with low coupling.
main_text: Specific Design Patterns. Class hierarchies with low coupling (if time permits). This section introduces common design patterns including Strategy, Factory, and Iterator.
notes_text: Design patterns are proven solutions to recurring design problems. They leverage inheritance and polymorphism to achieve loose coupling and flexibility.

title: Design Patterns Overview
summary: Introduces design patterns as common modular code practices, categorized into Creational, Structural, and Behavioral patterns.
main_text: Design patterns are common software practices to create modular code, often using inheritance and polymorphism. Researchers studied software development processes and actual code to see if there were common patterns that were often used. The most well-known study resulted in a book by four authors affectionately known as the 'Gang of Four' (or GoF): Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides. Creational Patterns: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype. Structural Patterns: Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Bridge, Composite, Flyweight, Proxy. Behavioral Patterns: Iterator, Mediator, Chain of Responsibility, Command, State, Memento, Observer, Template Method, Strategy, Visitor, Interpreter.
notes_text: The Gang of Four book is one of the most influential software engineering books. These patterns provide a shared vocabulary for discussing design solutions. Not all patterns need to be memorized, but understanding the categories and a few key patterns (Strategy, Factory, Iterator) is valuable.

title: Understanding UML Relationships
summary: Introduces UML class diagrams for depicting inheritance and composition relationships between classes.
main_text: UML (Unified Modeling Language) is often used to depict software designs and object relationships. UML can be very detailed and specific, whereas we may often use a basic subset to communicate our SW design. We'll generally just use generic inheritance and composition relationships. The basic UML diagram shows: A Client class with an Interface* member (dashed arrow for composition/dependency). An Interface class (abstract) with solid inheritance arrows pointing up from Concrete ObjectA and Concrete ObjectB to the Interface. This pattern shows a client depending on an abstract interface, with concrete implementations inheriting from it.
notes_text: UML provides a standardized visual language for software design. The key arrows to know: solid line with hollow triangle = inheritance (derived points to base), dashed arrow = dependency/usage, solid line with diamond = composition.

images.description: UML class diagram showing Client box with Interface* member, connected by dashed arrow to Interface box. Below Interface, two boxes (Concrete ObjectA and Concrete ObjectB) with solid inheritance arrows pointing up to Interface.

title: Strategy Pattern
summary: Introduces the Strategy pattern: abstracting an interface to allow alternative algorithmic approaches to be swapped at runtime.
main_text: The Strategy pattern abstracts an interface to allow alternative approaches. It is a fairly classic polymorphism idea. In a video game the AI may take different strategies. It decouples AI logic from how moves are chosen and provides for alternative approaches to determine what move to make. The pattern: A Client has a Interface* member (e.g. AI has MoveBehavior* if). The Interface (e.g. MoveBehavior) defines makeMove(). Concrete implementations (e.g. Aggressive Behavior, Random Behavior) inherit from the interface and implement makeMove() differently. Recall the 'Shapes' example/exercise from class/lab: a program that dealt with abstract shape class rather than concrete rectangles, circles, etc. The program could now deal with any new shape provided it fit the interface.
notes_text: The Strategy pattern is one of the most commonly used patterns. It allows behavior to be selected at runtime by assigning different concrete strategy objects. The key benefit: the client code doesn't change when new strategies are added. Just create a new derived class and assign it.

images.description: Two UML diagrams: top shows generic Strategy pattern with Client, Interface, and two Concrete Objects. Bottom shows specific example with AI class, MoveBehavior interface with makeMove(), and Aggressive Behavior and Random Behavior as concrete implementations.

title: On Your Own - Additional Design Patterns
summary: Lists additional design patterns (Observer, Proxy, Template Method, Adapter) for self-study with resource links.
main_text: Design Patterns to explore on your own: Observer, Proxy, Template Method, Adapter. Questions to try to answer: How does it make the design more modular (loosely coupled)? When/why would you use the pattern? Resources: http://sourcemaking.com/, http://www.vincehuston.org/dp/, http://www.oodesign.com/.
notes_text: These four patterns are commonly encountered in practice. Observer is used in event systems and UI frameworks. Proxy wraps access to objects. Template Method defines algorithm skeletons. Adapter converts one interface to another.

title: Review Questions - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing review questions for inheritance and polymorphism details.
main_text: Review Questions. Practice problems covering inheritance access, protected members, and private inheritance effects.
notes_text: These review questions test understanding of access specifiers, inheritance types, and their interactions.

title: Inheritance Review 1 - Questions
summary: Review questions testing whether Student has/can access name_ and id_, and what changes if private inheritance is used.
main_text: Given Person with public constructor and get_name()/get_id(), and private string name_, int id_. Student : public Person with public methods and private int major_, double gpa_. T/F: A student object has a name_ and id_ member. T/F: Code from the Student class can access name_ and id_. What could you change to flip the T/F answer? What would change if Student inherited Person through private inheritance? In main(): Student s1("Amanda", 12345, 1); cout << s1.get_name() << endl;
notes_text: These are fundamental comprehension questions. A Student object DOES have name_ and id_ (they exist in memory), but Student code CANNOT access them directly because they are private to Person. To flip the answer: change Person's access specifier to protected or public.

title: Inheritance Review 2 - Questions
summary: Fill-in-the-blank review: inheritance defines _____ relationship, composition defines _____ relationship, protected accessible to _____ but not _____.
main_text: Inheritance defines an _______ relationship between classes. Composition defines a _________ relationship between two objects. Protected access makes members accessible to ____________ but still not to _________________.
notes_text: Answers: inheritance = is-a, composition = has-a, protected accessible to derived/child classes but still not to external/3rd-party clients.

title: CS 104 Examples - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing advanced examples that preview CS104-level inheritance and polymorphism usage.
main_text: CS 104 Examples. This section shows practical applications of inheritance and polymorphism in search engine design, demonstrating Strategy and Factory patterns.
notes_text: These examples bridge CS103 concepts to more advanced CS104 material, showing how design patterns are applied in real projects.

title: Your Search Engine - Strategy Pattern Applied
summary: Applies the Strategy pattern to a search engine with AND, OR, and Normal search modes as interchangeable implementations.
main_text: Think about your class project and where you might be able to use the strategy pattern. AND, OR, Normal Search. The pattern: A client class has a SearchMode* if member. SearchMode is the interface with a search() method. ANDSearch, ORSearch, and SingleSearch inherit from SearchMode and implement search() differently. Client code: cin >> sType; SearchMode* s; if(sType == "AND") s = new ANDSearch; else if(sType == "OR") s = new ORSearch; else s = new SingleSearch; getline(cin, searchWords); s->search(searchWords);. The same client code works with any search mode through polymorphism.
notes_text: This is a practical application of the Strategy pattern for a search engine. The search algorithm is abstracted behind the SearchMode interface. Adding a new search mode (e.g. DIFF search) only requires creating a new derived class and updating the if/else creation code. The search execution code remains unchanged.

images.description: UML diagram showing client with SearchMode* member, SearchMode interface with search() method, and three concrete implementations (ANDSearch, ORSearch, SingleSearch) inheriting from SearchMode.

title: Factory Pattern
summary: Introduces the Factory pattern: abstracting object creation into a factory function so clients don't need to know concrete types.
main_text: A function, class, or static function of a class used to abstract creation. Rather than making your client construct objects (via 'new', etc.), abstract that functionality so that it can be easily extended without affecting the client. The pattern: A Client uses a Factory class which has a makeItem() method. The Factory creates objects that conform to the Item interface. makeItem(int type) uses if/else to return the appropriate concrete type: if(type==A) return new ItemA; else if(type==B) return new ItemB;. The client only knows about Item*, not the concrete types. Usage: Item* i = factory.makeItem(type);
notes_text: The Factory pattern centralizes object creation logic. The benefit is that the client code never uses 'new ConcreteType' directly, so adding new types only requires updating the factory, not every piece of client code. This is especially powerful when combined with the Strategy pattern.

images.description: UML diagram showing Client connected to Factory (with makeItem() method) and Item interface. Factory creates Items. Concrete ItemA and ItemB inherit from Item. Code snippet shows makeItem using if/else to return appropriate type.

title: Factory Example - Search Engine
summary: Combines Strategy and Factory patterns for the search engine, with SearchFactory creating SearchMode objects polymorphically.
main_text: We can pair up our search strategy objects with a factory to allow for easy creation of new approaches. Factory: class SearchFactory with static SearchMode* create(string type) that returns new ANDSearch for "AND", new ORSearch for "OR", else new SingleSearch. Search Interface: class SearchMode with virtual search(set<string> searchWords) = 0;. Concrete Search: class AndSearch : public SearchMode implements search(). Client code: cin >> sType; SearchMode* s = SearchFactory::create(sType); getline(cin, searchWords); s->search(searchWords);. The client is now completely decoupled from the concrete search types.
notes_text: This example shows how Strategy and Factory work together. The Factory encapsulates the creation logic (the if/else chain). The Strategy pattern provides the polymorphic interface. The client code is reduced to just two lines: create via factory and call search. Adding a new search mode requires only updating the factory and creating a new derived class.

title: Factory Example - Adding New Search Modes
summary: Shows the benefit of Factory pattern: adding a new DIFFSearch mode requires no changes to client code.
main_text: The benefit is now I can add new search modes without the client changing or even recompiling. The SearchFactory is updated to add: else if(type == "DIFF") return new DIFFSearch;. A new class DIFFSearch : public SearchMode implements search(set<string> searchWords). The client code remains exactly the same: cin >> sType; SearchMode* s = SearchFactory::create(sType); getline(cin, searchWords); s->search(searchWords);. The client does not need to change or recompile when new search modes are added.
notes_text: This demonstrates the Open/Closed Principle in action. The system is open for extension (new search modes) but closed for modification (client code doesn't change). Only the factory needs a one-line update, and a new derived class is created. This is the gold standard for extensible OO design.

title: Iterator Pattern
summary: Introduces the Iterator pattern that decouples data organization from traversal, allowing uniform access to BSTs, lists, and arrays.
main_text: The Iterator pattern decouples organization of data in a collection from the client who wants to iterate over and access just the data. Data could be in a BST, linked list, or array. Client just needs to: Allocate an iterator [it = collection.begin()]. Dereference the iterator to access data [*it]. Increment/decrement the iterator [++it]. The iterator hides the internal structure of the collection, providing a uniform interface for traversal regardless of the underlying data structure.
notes_text: The Iterator pattern is so fundamental that it is built into the C++ Standard Library (STL). Every container (vector, list, map, set) provides iterators that work with the same interface. This allows generic algorithms (sort, find, for_each) to work with any container.

title: Solutions - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing solutions to the review questions.
main_text: Solutions. This section provides answers to the review questions from this unit.
notes_text: Students should attempt the review questions before consulting these solutions.

title: Inheritance Review 1 - Solutions
summary: Provides solutions: Student HAS name_/id_ (True), but CANNOT access them directly (False because private). Changing to protected flips it.
main_text: T/F: A student object has a name_ and id_ member. TRUE - a Student inherits and physically contains these members. T/F: Code from the Student class can access name_ and id_. FALSE - they are private to Person, so Student cannot access them directly. What could you change to flip the T/F answer? Changing Person's access specifier to protected or public. Regardless of how Student inherits, name_ and id_ will be private to the Student class if Person declared them private. What would change if Student inherited Person through private inheritance? External clients (like main) would not be able to access the inherited members (from Person) of a Student object. s1.get_name() would fail.
notes_text: Key distinction: having a member (it exists in memory) vs. being able to access it (compile-time access control). The access specifier in the BASE class determines what the DERIVED class can see. The inheritance type determines what EXTERNAL code can see.

title: Inheritance Review 2 - Solutions
summary: Provides solutions: inheritance = is-a, composition = has-a, protected accessible to derived/child class but not external/3rd-party clients.
main_text: Inheritance defines an is-a relationship between classes. Composition defines a has-a relationship between two objects. Protected access makes members accessible to a derived/child class but still not to external/3rd-party clients.
notes_text: These three concepts form the foundation of OO design with inheritance: is-a (inheritance), has-a (composition), and protected (selective access). Understanding these relationships is essential for making correct design decisions.
